strengths: The paper substantially extends prior work on sinusoidal number representations (Kadlcík et al., 2025; Zhou et al., 2024; Kantamneni and Tegmark, 2025) by providing the first quantitative cross-model (RSA, Fourier IoU) and cross-layer assessment of alignment, moving beyond qualitative observations in earlier studies.

The proposed param-sin probe is a simple, well-motivated architectural improvement over the prior sin probe: strictly constraining the classifier to d sine waves with learnable frequency, amplitude, and phase yields consistent accuracy gains, and is validated against several baseline probe types from the literature.

The study is notably broader in scope than prior work: six models from three families across layers, four natural-language domains (~700K contexts), four arithmetic operations, multi-token numbers, and ordinal data types. The finding that probes trained on natural-language contexts generalize across context distributions while synthetic-context probes do not is a practically important and novel observation.

Section 4 provides convincing mechanistic evidence: the TunedLens comparison showing general-purpose tools underestimate superposed numeric information, the layer-wise error analysis (Table 2: models often achieve correct results internally that do not surface), and activation steering toward sinusoidal patterns correcting up to 30-42% of multiplication/division errors.

Reproducibility is well supported: probe architecture and hyperparameters are documented in Appendix B, dataset specifications in Table 3, and the authors state all code and probes are publicly released. A limitations section and LLM-usage disclosure are included.

The writing is clear, the experimental narrative is well organized, and the central claims (universality of sinusoidal structure; necessity of specialized explainability tooling) are directly connected to the reported experiments.
weaknesses: Some claims are stronger than the evidence supports. 'Almost perfectly universal' rests on three model families, all English-centric, all under 30B parameters; the Phi family in particular shows weaker alignment (Figure 1), which softens the universality claim. The authors acknowledge this in Limitations, but abstract-level language overstates it.

The inference from probe accuracy to representation structure has a logical gap: superior accuracy of sinusoidal probes over linear/binary/log baselines indicates sinusoidality is a good (possibly best-available linear-ish) description, but does not strictly prove the representation is sinusoidal, especially since Zhu et al. (2025) argue linear probes suffice. The 'lower bound' framing partly addresses this but the paper at times treats probe fit as proof of mechanism.

In the steering experiments (Figure 9), results are reported with respect to the optimal interpolation factor α per layer, operation, and probe; this per-setup oracle selection likely inflates the reported error-correction gains and weakens the practical significance of the intervention. Similarly, the layer-removal intervention is extremely naive and the authors themselves note low absolute correct-prediction counts in lower layers limit applicability.

Evidence that sinusoidality determines output accuracy (§4.2) mixes correlational observations (differing sinusoidality of addition vs. multiplication embeddings, Appendix A.5) with interventional results; the causal chain would benefit from stronger controls or a more careful causal framing.

Several analyses rest on very small samples: leave-one-out evaluation on 7 weekdays, 12 months, 10 numerals yields near-ceiling differences of a few matches, and the zero-position blind spot of the probe parametrization (Limitations) affects all ordinal results.

Some experimental details are thin in the main text: probe training set sizes and number of held-out numbers per condition vary across experiments (e.g., 'hold out 100 numbers'), and the companion codebase is referenced for exact hyperparameters rather than fully specified; results also lack confidence intervals or multiple seeds in most figures.

Minor presentation issues: occasional typos ('the the observed sinusoidality', 'mechanistic evidence that sinusoidality is crucial'), and some figures (e.g., Figure 13 PCA heatmaps) are hard to interpret and contribute little.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant and active topic (numeric representations in LLMs) and positions itself reasonably well against prior work (Kadlcík et al., 2025; Zhou et al., 2024; Kantamneni and Tegmark, 2025), identifying concrete gaps such as the lack of natural-language-context evaluation and cross-model/cross-layer quantification.

The evaluation spans multiple models (OLMo 2, Llama 3, Phi 4 families, 1B–15B), multiple layers, and multiple context domains, with held-out splits by number value to test generalization rather than memorization.

The proposed param-sin probe is a sensible, strictly constrained architecture, and the reported comparisons against prior probe types (bin, lin, log, sin, TunedLens) are informative, particularly the demonstration that TunedLens systematically underestimates recoverable numeric information in multi-token numbers.

The combination of probing, cross-layer transfer, Fourier/RSA analyses, and steering interventions gives the central claims of sinusoidal universality multiple lines of supporting evidence, and appendices provide reasonable additional detail (component-wise probing, error tracking, dataset specification).
weaknesses: The core contribution is incremental. The central observation—that numeric representations are sinusoidal—is well established (Nanda et al., 2023; Zhou et al., 2024; Kadlcík et al., 2025; Kantamneni and Tegmark, 2025), and the new probe is a modest architectural refinement of Kadlcík et al.'s probe rather than a conceptual advance. The novelty reduces largely to (i) a parameterized sine probe, (ii) natural-language contexts, and (iii) applying known tools to new operations.

The central novelty claim ('first to analyze numeric processing in natural-language settings') is overstated: several of the 'natural language' datasets (MetaMathQA, DROP, AQuA-RAT) are synthetic or templated mathematical reasoning data, blurring the claimed distinction from prior synthetic settings; only a minority of contexts are genuinely natural text, and some are tiny (e.g., 50 legal-document dates).

Evidence for some headline claims is weaker than the rhetoric. The abstract claims sinusoidality 'mechanistically' leads to reduced arithmetic errors, but the steering experiments correct at most 30–42% of errors only on upper layers under per-setup optimal α, layer removal works in 4/6 cases, and division probing accuracy is only 5.9% in Table 2 — 'mechanistically prove' in the introduction is not warranted by this evidence.

The claim of 'almost perfectly universal' representations rests on just three model families, all English-centric and all under 30B parameters, with Phi notably less aligned; generalization of 'universal' claims from this sample is not supported, and the Limitations section concedes this while the body text continues to overclaim.

Reproducibility is incomplete: the code availability sentence in Appendix B literally ends with 'available at' followed by no URL, no seeds or variance over repeated probe fits are reported, and several experimental details (e.g., exact prompts, the k=63 selection criterion being partially post hoc, the IoU baseline construction) are underspecified. For a paper whose contribution is a probe plus methodology, this is a significant gap.

Some analyses are qualitative or post hoc: the k=63 cutoff is chosen as 'the highest k with perfect agreement', which invites selection concerns; first/last-layer failures are explained only through a sparsity hypothesis ('we hypothesize'); and the title's informal register ('and Here's Why You Should Care') is not matched by the rigor of the supporting evidence.

The ordinal-data section (§4.3) operates with 6–11 training examples per class and a known parametrization blind spot (zero/first position always wrong), so the reported near-perfect matches in Table 1 are hard to interpret as strong evidence rather than an artifact of the parametric form.

Writing quality is uneven: several sentences are grammatically flawed ('we can see that the param-sin probe performs comparable or better', 'that sinusoidality is crucial for models' accuracy'), and key figures (e.g., Figure 1 RSA heatmaps, Figure 9) are difficult to read at the provided resolution, impeding verification of claimed effects.

strengths: Comprehensive and well-motivated study: the paper systematically evaluates number representations across eight LLMs from three families (OLMo 2, Llama 3, Phi 4), quantifying cross-model similarity via RSA and Fourier-frequency IoU, extending prior qualitative observations (Zhou et al., 2024) into a quantitative result of near-perfect frequency agreement for number tokens.

The new param-sin probe (Eq. 2) is a clean, well-motivated architectural improvement over Kadlcík et al. (2025): it strictly enforces sinusoidal structure and directly optimizes frequency/phase/amplitude, and is shown to outperform prior probes in decoding accuracy, multi-token superposition analysis, and ordinal data (days, months) under extreme data scarcity.

The analysis in natural-language contexts (four domains, ~700K contexts, held-out number splits) is a genuine and practically important departure from prior work that used synthetic/single-token settings, and the demonstrated train/eval distribution mismatch (Figure 4) is a useful caution for the interpretability community.

Good causal-style evidence beyond probing: activation steering toward sinusoidal patch embeddings corrects up to 30–42% of arithmetic errors and outperforms the prior sin probe in nearly all setups; component-wise analysis (Fig. 17) and residual-stream attribution add mechanistic depth.

Good clarity overall: the paper is well written, figures generally support the claims, limitations are candidly discussed (model scope, English-centricity, probe blind spot at position 0), and code/data are stated to be released with exact hyperparameters, supporting reproducibility.

Relevance to ACL is clear: the findings directly question the practice of general-purpose interpretability tooling and demonstrate that tool choice (TunedLens vs. sinusoidal probes) can flip conclusions about what information models retain.
weaknesses: The causal claim that 'a precision of sinusoidality in the model's internal representation determines its output accuracy' is not fully established. Steering toward the probe-fitted sinusoidal pattern is effectively steering toward the correct answer's decoded value; without a control condition (e.g., steering toward a non-sinusoidal encoding of the same target, or patch embeddings fit to a linear probe), error reduction does not isolate sinusoidality as the operative factor. The layer-removal intervention is self-described as naive and its gains are modest and inconsistently applicable (4 of 6 cases, with negligible correct predictions in lower layers).

Some framing overreaches the evidence: 'almost perfectly universal' and 'mechanistically prove' are stronger than the supporting results; Phi models align less well (Fig. 1), the 5th-token superposition decays to near-zero accuracy, and division probing accuracy is low (5.9% in Table 2), which complicates the universality narrative in places.

The experimental scope is narrow in ways that limit generality: number range largely restricted to 0–999 (and up to ~10^18 for multi-token), three families, English-centric models, and single small models in several analyses (e.g., Figure 4 generalization study, Figure 6 TunedLens comparison). No statistical significance testing, confidence intervals, or multiple-seed results are reported for probe accuracies or steering gains.

Comparison baselines are somewhat asymmetric: the TunedLens 'conflicting account' (§4.1) is attributed to tool inefficiency, but alternative explanations (e.g., different target-token setups, calibration) are not fully ruled out; the probe comparison in Fig. 3 uses prior-work probes under configurations that may not be equally tuned.

Some analyses are thin or relegated to the appendix with limited discussion: the A.6 sparsity findings, the crossover behavior at k≈250 in Figure 10 (which weakens the number-vs-random contrast at higher k), and the A.8 layer-breaking results deserve more careful treatment given they qualify the headline claims.

Several figure/rendering and presentational issues (very small fonts in Figure 1 heatmaps, Figure 17 matrix legibility) and occasional imprecise writing ('proves', 'almost always outperform') slightly detract from clarity.
